To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Please read and share – the warning about fake blue tablets

Please don’t scroll past this, and please share it rather than just liking it. I’m putting what parents and teenagers need to know in one place.

The police warning is about blue tablets being sold as diazepam or “Xanax”. Some have been found to contain nitazenes, which are synthetic opioids and can be far stronger than heroin. Something can look like a tablet somebody recognises and still not be what they think it is.

If someone goes down, becomes extremely drowsy or can’t be woken properly, RING 999 STRAIGHT AWAY.

Don’t put them to bed to “sleep it off”. Don’t leave them on their own. Don’t wait hours because you’re panicking or worried about getting into trouble.

The warning signs listed by police include:
- extreme drowsiness
- pinpoint pupils, meaning very small pupils
- slow or noisy breathing
- blue lips

You don’t have to wait until every one of those signs is there, and you don’t need to know exactly what somebody has taken before calling. Stay with them, put them on their side if they’re breathing but unresponsive, and follow the 999 call handler’s instructions. If you know what they’ve taken, tell the paramedics honestly.

The police have said clearly in their warning: “Our priority is preserving life.” Please make sure your children know that. Making that call is the right thing to do, not something to be ashamed of.

The delay is what frightens me. Generally speaking, you hear about groups of mates panicking, putting somebody in bed and hoping they’ll come round, then ringing hours later when they still won’t wake. By then, their brain may have been without oxygen for too long. That is why “let them sleep it off” can be so dangerous.

Parents, please talk to your kids THIS week – not after half term, not when you find the perfect moment. I had the conversation with my 14-year-old over his tea last night. There were plenty of eye rolls, but he listened and asked me what pinpoint pupils meant. It doesn’t have to be a massive lecture, and you don’t need to pretend this could never affect your child or their friends. Just make sure they know: if somebody becomes unwell, ring 999 immediately and stay with them.

If you’re a teenager reading this, you might be frightened of your parents finding out, frightened of the police, or worried you’ll be blamed. Ring anyway. Being the person who makes that call could save your mate’s life.

There’s also something practical people can do. Naloxone nasal spray can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose. Brightpath drug & alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette, provides free nasal naloxone kits. Anyone can ask, no names are needed, and the training takes about 10 minutes. They’re open Monday to Friday, 10–4, with Thursdays open until 7. If somebody has naloxone and uses it, they still needs to ring 999 – waking up doesn’t mean an ambulance isn’t needed.

And can we please stop slagging kids off? Whatever anyone thinks about drugs, shaming young people and their parents helps nobody. If kids are convinced they’ll be judged or get into serious trouble, they’re less likely to ask for help. Scared kids not ringing is the whole problem. We can talk honestly about risks and choices without making anyone too frightened to save a friend.

Please share this so it reaches parents and teenagers who haven’t seen the police warning. A like is appreciated, but a share might actually get this in front of somebody who needs it.
